newsitem.title: FRANCE: Porsche puts future on the line with new Boxster.
newsitem.headline: Porsche puts future on the line with new Boxster.

text.p: German sports car maker Porsche, just recovering from near collapse in the early 1990s, is putting its future on the line with the debut of its first new car in nearly two decades -- the Boxster.

The two-seat cabriolet, being displayed at the Paris car show this week and due to hit German show rooms this month, will take its place along side the 911 model as the only two cars Porsche will produce.
The new Boxter has a heavy burden since it must sell every bit as well as the legendary 911 if the car maker is to continue its recovery, industry analysts said.

The Boxster's debut, which has been delayed by constent refinements, comes at a time of increasing competition for pricy roadster two-seat sports cars and promises to be a true test of Porsche's cachet in the luxury market place.
"This is a big moment for Porsche," said Peter Schmidt, analyst at Automotive Industry Data. "But Porsche has shown that it knows how to survive."

The Boxster is Porsche's first new car since 1977 when it launched the 928, one of a string of unsuccessful cars that, combined with a terrible U.S. sports car market in the late 1980s, brought the venerable German car maker to its knees.
Analysts said from what they have seen so far, the Boxster should be able to help Porsche's continue financial recovery.

The model, whose six-cylinder, liquid-cooled engine is located in the middle of the body, has won solid reviews from car magazines and test drivers who see it as a return to Porsche's time-honored successful formula of providing top performance and bold masculine lines.
"Some of Porsche's more recent models have gotton a reputation as 'hair-dresser cars'," Schmidt said. "Porsche drivers want to be Clint Eastwoods and the Boxster gives them that."

The car has already won orders about equal to the planned first year's production of about 15,000, or about as many of the 911s that Porsche hopes to sell. In its 1995-96 business year, Porsche made some 20,000 911s.

But the Boxster's standing is far from assured with BMW AG and Mercedes-Benz AG both recently debuting roadsters similar to the Boxster and costing well below the new Porsche's 75,000 marks ($49,220).

While number crunchers may debate the financial success of the Boxster, Germany's Auto Motor und Sport magazine, the bible of the German car industry, maybe summed up the car best in a recent cover story.
"With the Boxster you have a true Porsche with driving enjoyment similar to the 911. What more could you want?" ($1=1.5235 Mark)
